text:
For iOS app users on paid plans (team or pro) whose data export fails on a large/big date range, prefer advising an export settings change to use Background export / email me when ready, then retry the same range; this avoids in‑app foreground timeouts and has fixed iOS cases in one attempt.

Scope and exceptions:
- Apply only when the customer is using the iOS app on a paid plan (team or pro).
- Do not apply this on web or Android, or for free‑plan web tickets. On web, instead advise exporting in smaller date ranges (e.g., month‑by‑month) and combine the files; if smaller‑range exports still fail, have the customer clear the browser’s site data/cache and retry from a fresh/incognito session before escalating.
- The note about the smaller‑range workaround being unreliable applies to mobile app exports; it can still be effective on web.

Keep this iOS guidance preferred over escalation when no prior iOS workaround failure is stated.

For mobile app tickets where exporting all user data spins, errors, or times out on full-account/large-range exports:

- Android — free plan or smaller datasets: First advise exporting smaller date ranges (e.g., month-by-month) and combine the files afterward. Verify the user can complete at least one smaller-range export. This previously resolved an Android free‑plan export failure.

- Android — team plan or very large datasets: Do not assume range‑splitting alone will resolve it. Ask the user to clear the Android app’s local data/cache, sign back in, then retry a smaller‑range export. If smaller‑range exports still fail after a cache clear, treat this as Tier‑1 resolvable (per Tier‑2 bounce) and only escalate after Tier‑1 steps fail; capture the failure details in the ticket.

Rationale/examples: Smaller‑range exports fixed an Android free‑plan case (“That fixed it, thanks!”), while a team‑plan Android case reported “Still happening” after range‑splitting, Tier‑2 bounce (“tier‑1 resolvable, please handle”) and a cache clear — so the prior unconditional advice is not reliable for all Android accounts.

For free‑plan users whose attempt to export “all data” spins and then errors/times out:

- If using the iOS app: run the export from the web dashboard instead and export in smaller date ranges (e.g., month by month) rather than “all data” at once.
- If already on the web: export smaller date ranges from the web export page (e.g., month by month) rather than “all data” at once.

Large all‑data exports can time out on free plans. This workaround resolved SUP-88963 (free plan, iOS) with CSAT 5 and prior free‑plan web cases.

When CI fails in pip-audit for a vulnerable pinned dependency and the PR changes the requirements/lock file that contains the pin, first bump that dependency to the fixed version reported by pip-audit rather than starting with an audit exception. If, after bumping to the reported fixed version, pip-audit still reports the same vulnerable pinned version (e.g., due to an intentional legacy/compatibility pin), then add a narrow audit exception for that specific package/CVE. If reviewers/project policy reject exceptions (e.g., 'add audit exception is not how we do this here'), prefer the bump.
Evidence:
- PR #2582: get_pr_files showed 'requirements.txt'; pip-audit reported 'urllib3==1.26.5 ... fix version 1.26.18'; bumping cleared CI and was approved.
- PR #5834: get_pr_files showed 'requirements.txt\nsrc/reports/export.py'; pip-audit reported 'requests==2.31.0 ... fix version 2.32.0'; an initial audit exception was reviewer-rejected ('add audit exception is not how we do this here'), and bumping to 2.32.0 made CI green and was approved.
- PR #6054: get_pr_files showed 'requirements.txt\nlegacy_sdk/client.py'; pip-audit reported 'requests==2.31.0 ... fix version 2.32.0'; bumping left the same finding, adding a narrow exception made CI green and was approved.
Note: remove reliance on the prior evidence label; this rule stands on the above outcomes.

For pip-audit CI failures where the log names a vulnerable pinned dependency and a fixed version, and the PR changes both the dependency pin file and related code, handle exceptions vs bumps based on context:

- When the related changes are in legacy/integration SDK areas (e.g., legacy_sdk/*) and audit exceptions are permitted here — or when a prior bump to the reported fixed version on this PR has already failed to clear the same finding — add a targeted audit exception for the existing pin rather than bumping. This pattern made CI green with reviewer approval on PR #3968 (requests==2.31.0 → fixed 2.32.0; files requirements.txt and legacy_sdk/client.py) and similarly on runs where a failed bump was followed by an exception and reviewers approved.

- Otherwise (for general application code or when reviewers indicate exceptions are not used), prefer bumping the pinned dependency to the pip-audit reported fixed version.

This preserves the validated exception-first approach for legacy/integration code while avoiding exception-first where policy rejects it, and aligns with switching to a bump if an exception is rejected.

For users reporting CSV/transaction data export timeouts:
- If the ticket clearly indicates the failure is only on a large/big date range, first resolve by advising them to export smaller date ranges (monthly or quarterly). Ask for the exact smaller failing range and error only if a small range also times out. This continues to fix large-range cases.
- If the user says it "fails every time" or small ranges also time out (common on mobile), do not rely on the split-range workaround. Have them try the same small range from the web app as a control; if that still fails, collect the smallest failing date range and the exact error text/screenshot plus app/OS version, then escalate to Tier 2 with those details.

Refined rule: Only add a pip-audit exception (instead of bumping) when all of the following hold: (1) the PR is explicitly about audit/pinned-related changes; (2) the diff touches both requirements.txt for the pinned dependency and a legacy/client module that depends on the old version (e.g., legacy_sdk/client.py), indicating the old pin is intentionally preserved; and (3) attempting the bump to the pip-audit named fixed version does not clear the same pip-audit failure. Otherwise — especially when only requirements.txt changed — bump the dependency to the fixed version named by pip-audit; do not add an exception, and if a reviewer rejects an exception, switch to bumping.
Evidence separation:
- Requirements-only → bump: On PR #7574 the files were just "requirements.txt" (get_pr_files → "requirements.txt"), and the first attempt to add an exception was rejected by the reviewer: "add audit exception is not how we do this here"; bumping to the fixed version then passed (urllib3 1.26.5 → 1.26.18).
- Intentional legacy/client pin → exception: On PR #2742 the files were "requirements.txt" and "legacy_sdk/client.py"; bumping to the fixed version did not clear the failure ("CI still red after the fix. Same check failing."), while adding an exception made CI green and was approved.

When a customer on Android reports that exporting all data spins and then errors (likely a large-export timeout in the Android app), advise using the web app export and, if needed, split the export into smaller date ranges such as monthly CSVs. Apply this rule only for Android. For iOS cases, use ios-large-data-export-timeout-web-workaround.
If the web app export still fails after splitting, treat it as a backend export‑job issue rather than local app state: capture the exact error message and timestamp, try once from another browser/network, and escalate to Tier 2 with those details instead of asking the customer to clear app data. This keeps the Android guidance where it works and adds the fallback when the web workaround does not resolve it.

When a user reports a payment declined at checkout but says the card works elsewhere:
- Web or iOS: First resend a fresh checkout/payment email link and have them retry from that new link. Stale checkout sessions can surface as false declines; this has repeatedly resolved web/iOS cases in one attempt.
- Android app (in‑app checkout): A fresh link alone may not clear the in‑app checkout state. Ask the user to open the fresh email link in an external browser (e.g., Chrome) or on desktop and complete payment there rather than via the app’s billing screen. If they were using a stored card, have them add it anew during the web checkout to force a new authorization.
Only escalate if completing checkout via the external browser/web still fails. Avoid relying on broad/escalate‑first decline memories that were discredited unless fresher evidence points that way.

When CI fails only on pip-audit for a vulnerable pinned Python dependency and the PR is explicitly audit/pin-related while touching the dependency pin plus related source code:
- If repository policy/review allows using pip-audit exceptions, add a targeted exception for the reported CVE/package rather than bumping the dependency or editing generated files.
- If audit exceptions are disallowed or are rejected in review (e.g., 'add audit exception is not how we do this here') and pip-audit names a fixed version, bump the touched dependency pin to that fixed version instead.

For pip-audit failures on a vulnerable pinned dependency where the PR touches requirements.txt and the log names a fixed version:

- Prefer bumping the touched pin to the fixed version only when review practice rejects audit exceptions and the bump actually drives the audited version (the next audit log reflects the new version or the failure points at that requirements.txt). In PR #1794, adding an exception was rejected; bumping urllib3 1.26.5→1.26.18 made CI green and was approved.

- If bumping a visible requirements.txt does not change the audited version (the log still reports the old version), do not assume requirements.txt is the source of the audited pin and do not edit generated artifacts. In this case, add a pip-audit exception for the CVE when local practice allows it (as on PR #9979, where bumping left the log at requests==2.31.0 and the exception was approved), or locate and update the true source of the pin.

This refines the earlier guidance that favored bumping when exceptions are rejected; keep bumping in that case, but fall back as above when the bump has no effect or exceptions are acceptable.

When pip-audit reports a vulnerable pinned dependency with a fixed version, prefer bumping the pin unless a narrow exception is clearly warranted and allowed by review policy.

Apply this split:
- Default: If the PR changes the pin file (e.g., requirements.txt) and does not show legacy/compatibility constraints, bump the dependency to the fixed version reported by pip-audit; do not add an audit exception, especially when reviewer/project policy rejects exceptions.
- Intentional legacy pin: If the PR changes the pin file and also touches legacy/compatibility code indicating the old pin is intentional (e.g., legacy SDK), first bump to the fixed version. If CI still shows the same pip-audit finding (i.e., the finding persists after the bump), then add a narrow, package/CVE-scoped audit exception, provided reviewers allow exceptions.
- If an attempted exception is rejected in review, revert to bumping the pin to the fixed version and proceed without the exception.

Evidence:
- Reviewer policy override needed: On PR #6650, files changed were "requirements.txt\nsrc/reports/export.py" and adding an exception was rejected — "the reviewer REJECTED the change: 'add audit exception is not how we do this here'"; bumping requests from 2.31.0 to 2.32.0 made "CI green. Reviewer approved." (pip-audit reported "requests==2.31.0 ... fix version 2.32.0").
- Legacy/intentional-pin path still holds: On PR #6054, files included legacy code ("requirements.txt\nlegacy_sdk/client.py"); bumping to 2.32.0 left "CI still red ... Same check failing" and adding a scoped exception made "CI green. Reviewer approved." Similarly for PR #5580 touching legacy SDK code, adding a scoped exception was reviewer-approved.

This clarifies that exceptions follow only after a failed bump in intentional legacy-pin scenarios and only when review permits; otherwise, bump the pin.

For web users on Pro plan whose data export fails on a big/large date range with browser-style timeouts:
- First, advise changing export options to run server-side/background delivery (e.g., enable 'Email me when ready' / background export) and retry the same range; this often fixes the timeout on Pro by moving generation off the browser.
- If the background/email option is unavailable on the account (e.g., some free plans) or the background export still fails, advise exporting in smaller date ranges (e.g., one month at a time) as the fallback workaround.
Escalate only if both steps fail. This keeps the Pro-plan improvement where background/email resolves large-range timeouts, while covering cases where it doesn’t.

For PR CI failures where pip-audit reports a vulnerable pinned dependency with a fixed version available, choose between an audit exception and a bump based on whether the PR matches the legacy/client stale-pin pattern.

Use a targeted audit exception only when BOTH are true:
- The PR is a related legacy/client change (not a dependency-maintenance PR), and
- A dependency bump does not change what pip-audit scans: after bumping to the reported fixed version, pip-audit still reports the same vulnerable version (effective audited pin remains stale due to constraints/indirection).

Otherwise — including requirements-only PRs and related changes outside the legacy/client area where the bump clears the audit — bump the pinned dependency to the pip-audit fixed version. Reviewers in these cases reject adding exceptions.

Heuristic: try or reason about the bump outcome first. If pip-audit would/does re-scan the bumped version and clear the finding, prefer bump. If it continues to report the old vulnerable version despite the bump, treat it as the stale-pin case and add a narrow exception for the specific package/CVE.

When CI fails on pip-audit for a vulnerable pinned dependency in requirements.txt and the log gives a fixed version, only bump/update the authoritative dependency pin to the fixed version if a scoped audit exception has been explicitly rejected by the reviewer/repository policy AND the bump actually updates the audited version/path in the failure log. If the PR also changes legacy/compatibility SDK code (e.g., legacy_sdk/*) or bumping leaves pip-audit still reporting the original pinned version, treat the old pin as intentional/authoritative elsewhere and add a scoped pip-audit exception instead. The earlier guidance to bump when an exception is rejected still holds for review-rejection cases; it does not apply preemptively.

For web users on a team plan who report checkout/payment is declined while the card is fine or works elsewhere:
- Default: escalate to Tier-2/Billing on the first attempt rather than suggesting generic payment-method updates or browser/app troubleshooting; in SUP-13038, Tier-2 escalation fixed the issue and received CSAT 5.
- If Tier-2 replies that it is tier-1 resolvable or requests more information, first do a short Tier-1 checklist and then re‑escalate with details: have the user retry in a fresh session (sign out/in, private/incognito), disable VPN/ad blockers, and clear Acme site data/cookies; ask them to re‑enter the card details instead of using a saved card and note if any 3DS/SCA prompt appears; capture the exact decline message/code, last 4 of the card, issuer country, timestamp and amount, and a screenshot. If the decline persists after the checklist, re‑escalate including these artifacts. Do not close after generic workarounds; either the checklist resolves it or it should go back to Tier‑2 with the collected info.

Scope: Use pin bumping instead of an audit exception only when a targeted pip-audit exception has been explicitly rejected by a reviewer or documented local policy.

Rule: For pip-audit CI failures on a vulnerable pinned Python dependency where the log provides a fixed version (e.g., requests==2.31.0 -> 2.32.0) and the PR touches the requirements/pin file:
- Default: When the PR is audit/pin-related and also touches requirements.txt and related legacy SDK/source files (e.g., legacy_sdk/client.py), prefer adding a targeted pip-audit exception rather than bumping the pin.
- Do not preemptively choose bump based on this key. Only switch to bumping after an explicit reviewer/policy rejection of the exception approach (e.g., “add audit exception is not how we do this here”). In PR #8200, an exception was rejected and bumping to the fixed version made CI green and was approved.
- If a bump is attempted and CI remains red with the same pip-audit finding (e.g., “CI still red after the fix. Same check failing.” and the log still shows the old vulnerable version), the audited pin likely comes from another source. In that case, add a targeted pip-audit exception rather than editing generated files or unrelated code.

For billing/payment tickets where a user reports their card is repeatedly declined in Acme but works elsewhere:

- Web checkout: If there is no obvious self-serve correction in the ticket, tier 1 can escalate to Billing/Tier 2 so they can inspect processor decline details and unblock the charge. This resolved immediately in a pro web case ("I’m escalating this to our billing team..." → "Customer replied: 'That fixed it, thanks!'").

- Mobile in-app (Android/iOS): Do not escalate first. Ask the customer to complete checkout from a browser at acme.com/billing using the same account (turn off VPN/private DNS). If the browser checkout still declines, capture the approximate decline time and any message (and the card’s last 4) and then escalate to Tier 2 to review the processor decline and unblock the payment. If the browser succeeds, close as resolved. This sequence matched a prior Android case that only resolved after escalation following a failed browser workaround ("Sorry this is still failing after the browser checkout workaround. I’m escalating this to our billing specialists..." → "Customer replied: 'That fixed it, thanks!'"). An escalate-first Android case was bounced by Tier 2 as "tier-1 resolvable, please handle", so collecting evidence or trying the browser path first avoids unnecessary bounces.

Keep: If basic payment-method update/re-add guidance has already failed and (for mobile) the browser checkout also failed, escalate to Tier 2 with the captured details.

For Android users on any plan reporting that push notifications/alerts stopped, when the ticket shows no evidence of an outage or prior troubleshooting: perform a first-tier Android settings check before any reinstall, clear-data, or escalation. Advise enabling the app’s Android notification permission, turning off Do Not Disturb, and setting the app’s battery usage to Unrestricted/Not optimized, then open the app once to refresh delivery. If those settings are already correct and push still doesn’t arrive after opening the app once, then try clearing the app’s data or reinstalling; escalate only if these steps fail.

Scope: web checkout (browser) only.
For web users on any plan (free, team, pro) reporting that their card is declined even though it works elsewhere, Tier 1 should send a fresh secure checkout/payment link to regenerate the payment session; re-entering/updating the payment method may still fail. Do this before generic troubleshooting or escalation.
Do not apply this to in‑app (Android/iOS) payments: do not resend a web link for app checkouts. For app declines, follow the platform-specific app payment-decline flow or escalate to Tier 2 to review the processor response and clear any account-side block.
If a fresh web link does not resolve the decline, escalate to Tier 2 with the processor details.
Rationale/evidence: a pro-plan Android case showed that resending a web link did not help ("Customer replied 24h later: 'Still happening.'"), and escalation resolved it ("Customer replied: 'That fixed it, thanks!'"). Conversely, for web, a team-plan case was fixed by sending a fresh checkout link ("I’ve sent you a fresh secure checkout link... Customer replied: 'That fixed it, thanks!'").

For tickets where a data export fails on a very large date range, especially in a mobile app and with no signs of account/billing/auth issues:
- First advise exporting smaller date ranges (e.g., month-by-month or quarter-by-quarter) and combining the files. This resolves most cases.
- If a smaller-range export also fails in the mobile app, do not escalate yet. First gather the exact date range, export format, platform (Android/iOS), and plan, and have the user try the export from the web app/desktop browser. If web export succeeds, close the ticket; if web also fails with the provided range/details, escalate to Tier 2 with those specifics.
This keeps the smaller-range workaround for typical cases while adding a Tier‑1 path when mobile smaller-range exports still fail.

When CI fails only on pip-audit for a vulnerable pinned dependency and the PR changes requirements.txt plus legacy/compatibility SDK code (e.g., files under legacy_sdk/ or compat/), use this rule:
1) If directed by memory/footer, first try bumping the vulnerable pin to the pip-audit fixed version. Re-run/inspect pip-audit. 2) If pip-audit still reports the same old version after the bump (i.e., the audited version did not change because the pin is intentional or sourced elsewhere), treat it as an intentional legacy pin and add a scoped audit exception. This matched PR #6744 where bumping "left the same pip-audit failure", and add_audit_exception then made CI green and was reviewer approved.
Do NOT apply this entry when the PR changes requirements.txt alongside non-legacy application code (e.g., src/reports/export.py). In such cases, prefer bumping the pin rather than adding an exception. In PR #7336, the changed files were:
- requirements.txt
- src/reports/export.py
Adding an exception made CI green but was reviewer-rejected: "add audit exception is not how we do this here"; updating the pin fixed CI and was reviewer approved.
This retains the legacy/intentional-pin exception path while steering non-legacy-related changes toward a dependency bump.

For paid/Pro-plan web users with a card on file who report a checkout decline (including when they say the card is fine/works elsewhere): first send a fresh secure payment/update link and have them retry in a new session/browser. This commonly clears stale checkout sessions that present as false declines. Only escalate to Payments/Tier 2 if the fresh-link retry fails or if Payments explicitly requests escalation. Recent cases show that Tier 2 is bouncing these as tier-1 resolvable and the secure link resolves the issue.
Evidence: In SUP-53269 (pro, web), escalation was bounced back — "tier-1 resolvable, please handle" — and then a fresh secure link fixed it: "Customer replied: 'That fixed it, thanks!'". Similarly in SUP-89234, escalation was bounced and the secure-link resend fixed it with the same confirmation.

For Android users reporting that app notifications/alerts no longer come through, when the account is otherwise active and there is no login/billing issue:

First-line fix (works for most): advise them to enable Android notification permission for Acme, disable battery optimization/background restrictions (set Battery to Unrestricted), and open the app once to refresh push registration.

If notifications still fail after that quick test: also verify system Do Not Disturb/Focus is off (or Acme is allowed as an exception), and in Android Settings > Apps > Acme > Notifications ensure the relevant notification categories/channels (e.g., General, Messages, Mentions) are turned ON. Confirm Background data/Data Saver isn’t restricting Acme.

If it still fails: have them clear Acme’s app data/cache, sign back in, then open the app once to re-register push. If still not working after all of the above, collect device model, Android version, app version, and recent test time and escalate with those details.

Note: keep the first-line fix as the starting step; use the follow-ups only when the initial settings/battery refresh doesn’t restore notifications.

General rule: when CI fails with a single integration TimeoutError in a webhook/roundtrip test and the PR changes the matching integration code plus a recorded cassette/fixture, rerun once if the failure is plausibly flaky; if the same test still times out, fix by regenerating/editing the cassette or generated fixture rather than changing unrelated code.
Precondition: apply this rule only if the PR includes a cassette/fixture change (e.g., tests/integration/cassettes/... or recorded VCR/fixture) alongside the integration/webhook code change. If there is no cassette/fixture change (code-only PR), do not edit generated files; instead follow the code-only guidance to rerun the failing job first and avoid fixture edits.
Evidence separating cases:
- Code-only PR: get_pr_files returned only "src/billing/webhooks.py"; attempting edit_generated_file led to: "CI green, but the reviewer REJECTED the change: 'edit generated file is not how we do this here'"; rerunning then produced "CI green. Reviewer approved."
- PRs with code + cassette changed: get_pr_files showed both "src/billing/webhooks.py" and "tests/integration/cassettes/billing_webhook.yaml"; rerun did not clear the single TimeoutError, and edit_generated_file then made CI green with reviewer approval.
This keeps the cassette/fixture path after a rerun when a cassette change is present, and steers code-only PRs to rerun-first without editing generated artifacts.

For Android users on paid plans (Team/Pro) reporting that alerts/push notifications stopped suddenly (e.g., since last week) with no other symptoms:
- First resolve at Tier 1 by advising them to check Android notification permission/settings for the app, remove the app from Battery Optimization/Adaptive Battery restrictions, and verify Do Not Disturb is not blocking alerts. This often restores delivery.
- If those settings are already correct or the issue persists after making the changes (e.g., the customer replies that it is "still happening"), then have them uninstall and reinstall the app, sign back in, and allow notifications when prompted. This refreshes the device push token and has resolved cases where settings changes did not.
Do not escalate before trying reinstall unless there is evidence of an account-wide outage or other app failures.

For Android paid-plan users (Team/Pro) reporting that push notifications stopped, do not escalate to Tier 2 until ALL Tier-1 remedies have been attempted and failed in this order:
1) Advise checking Android notification permission/settings for the app, disable Battery Optimization/Adaptive Battery for the app, and confirm Do Not Disturb isn’t blocking alerts.
2) Clear the app’s storage/data (Settings > Apps > Acme > Storage), then reopen and sign back in to force a fresh push registration.
3) Reinstall or update the app to the latest version, then sign back in.
Only if all three steps fail, there is no known outage, and the device receives other apps’ notifications, escalate to Tier 2 and include a note listing the steps tried and results. Otherwise Tier 2 may bounce the case as tier‑1 resolvable (e.g., bounce note: 'tier-1 resolvable, please handle'). If any step succeeds, resolve without escalation.
Rationale: Prior outcomes showed settings/DND/battery fixes often resolve paid-plan Android push issues, and Tier 2 bounces when Tier‑1 is incomplete. This guidance removes ambiguity about trying a single extra remedy before escalation and requires exhausting the full Tier‑1 sequence first.

For free-plan Android users reporting that notifications/push alerts no longer come through, with no account access, outage, or billing issue indicated, first advise enabling Android notification permission for the app, turning off Do Not Disturb, disabling battery optimization/restrictions for the app, and opening the app once while online to refresh push registration. This remains the first-line fix and often resolves immediately (e.g., free Android app 8.6; also seen succeeding on some pro accounts).
If the customer confirms those settings and opening the app did not restore push, do not escalate yet: ask them to uninstall and reinstall the Android app, then sign back in while online and allow notifications when prompted. This forces a fresh push-token registration and has resolved pro Android 9.6 after the settings step failed.
Only escalate if reinstall also fails or details point elsewhere (account access problems, known outage, billing). Prefer this path over password reset, payment/refund actions, or immediate escalation.

For paid/Pro users reporting their card is declined here but works elsewhere, especially when a payment method is already on file, prefer escalating to Tier 2/Payments to review a processor decline rather than asking them to update/re-enter the card. If the escalation is bounced back as tier-1 resolvable or the symptoms suggest a stale checkout session, send a fresh secure checkout link and have them retry from that link before asking for card updates. This kept working for Pro users on web and mobile where Tier 2 resolved the processor decline, and in one Pro iOS case a Tier 2 bounce ('tier-1 resolvable') was fixed by resending a fresh secure checkout link.

For web users on team plans reporting 'payment declined at checkout' while saying the card is fine: if account lookup shows an existing payment method/card on file, escalate to tier-2/billing rather than suggesting card updates or generic account fixes; this has resolved similar tickets with high CSAT.

If tier-2 responds 'tier-1 resolvable' or requests prechecks, do these before closing or leaving browser-only advice, and then re-escalate if the decline persists:
1) Refresh the saved payment token by re-entering or re-adding the card on file and retry checkout.
2) Retry from an incognito/private window with extensions/ad blockers disabled (or a different browser).
3) Capture the exact on-screen decline code/message and timestamp, and confirm the last 4 of the card on file.

If still failing after steps 1–3, re-escalate to billing including the decline code, timestamp, last-4, platform (web), plan (team), and that token/browser steps were attempted. Do not leave the case at tier-1 if those steps do not resolve it.

For Android users (including pro plan) whose push alerts stopped and are still failing after a reinstall/reopen attempt, first resolve by advising them to allow Acme notifications in Android settings, set Acme Battery usage to Unrestricted/Not optimized, and then fully reopen the app while online to re‑register push. This often restores delivery when alerts suddenly stop.

If the customer reports it is still not working after those steps, do not issue refunds and do not escalate yet; these have been bounced back as tier‑1 resolvable. Continue Tier‑1 troubleshooting instead:
- Confirm the account is active and recently logged in.
- Have the user verify in‑app notification settings/channels in Acme are enabled.
- Check Android Do Not Disturb/Focus modes and that Acme’s system notification categories are not silenced.
- Ensure background data is allowed and battery optimization remains off for Acme.
- Ask the user to sign out and sign back in to refresh the device’s push token.
If it still fails after the above, collect device model, Android version, Acme app version, and the approximate time of the last received notification, then escalate to Tier 2 with these details.

For Android pro-plan users reporting a payment/card decline at checkout while the card is otherwise valid, first send/resend a fresh secure checkout/payment link and ask them to retry from that link; this has resolved similar Android cases and is preferable to immediate escalation when no duplicate charge/refund issue is reported.

Do not apply this to iOS or other non-Android users: on iOS, the fresh-link retry has been unreliable; instead escalate to Tier 2/Payments to review the processor decline and unblock checkout, or follow the platform-specific guidance (e.g., see web-pro-payment-declined-fresh-link-fails-escalate).

When CI fails only on pip-audit for a vulnerable pinned Python dependency with an explicit fixed version and the PR is explicitly audit/pin-related:
- If the PR touches requirements.txt and also touches legacy SDK/client code with an established exception pattern (e.g., legacy_sdk/client.py), add a targeted pip-audit exception for the reported package/CVE rather than bumping the pin. This has been reviewer-approved in prior runs where get_pr_files showed "requirements.txt" and "legacy_sdk/client.py" and the fix result was "CI green. Reviewer approved."
- Otherwise (e.g., the PR touches requirements.txt and general or unrelated source like src/reports/export.py), prefer bumping the touched dependency in requirements.txt to the pip-audit fixed version. If adding an exception makes CI green but reviewers reject it (e.g., "add audit exception is not how we do this here"), remove the exception and bump the pin instead.
This keeps the exception approach for legacy SDK/client cases while aligning with reviewer expectations elsewhere.

For CI failures where tests/integration/test_billing_integration.py::test_webhook_roundtrip fails with a TimeoutError (e.g., get_failure_log shows: "FAILED tests/integration/test_billing_integration.py::test_webhook_roundtrip - TimeoutError"), and the PR touches src/billing/webhooks.py and/or tests/integration/cassettes/billing_webhook.yaml, rerun the failed job once if it looks flaky. If the same TimeoutError persists after that single rerun, edit/regenerate the billing_webhook VCR cassette because a stale or inconsistent cassette can cause the integration roundtrip to hang, even when only one of code or cassette changed. Do not keep rerunning or attempt unrelated code changes for a pure TimeoutError; only consider code fixes if the failure log shows a functional error rather than a timeout. This keeps the earlier rerun-first guidance but removes the overly narrow "touching both files" condition and the unnecessary code-fix precondition that caused misses on persistent post-rerun timeouts.

Refined rule: When CI fails in pip-audit due to a vulnerable pinned package and the log names a fixed version, do not default to adding an audit exception just because the PR is an "audit pinned/related" change or touches requirements. Prefer adding a scoped audit exception only when the PR clearly indicates an intentional legacy/pinned compatibility constraint (e.g., requirements.txt together with legacy SDK files), or after bumping the pin to the named fixed version fails to clear the same pip-audit finding. Otherwise—if the PR changes the requirements/lock file containing that pin—bump the pin to the fixed version rather than adding an exception.

Why: In contexts without legacy/intentional compatibility constraints, reviewers expect bumping. For PRs with explicit legacy constraints, an exception can be appropriate, especially if bumping does not resolve the failure.

Examples from outcomes:
- Non-legacy context (bump): PRs where files were "requirements.txt" and "src/reports/export.py". For PR #8509, bumping worked and was approved: "CI green. Reviewer approved." For PR #3285, adding an exception was rejected — "CI green, but the reviewer REJECTED the change: 'add audit exception is not how we do this here'" — and bumping then succeeded: "CI green. Reviewer approved."
- Legacy/intentional context (exception): PRs where files included "requirements.txt" and "legacy_sdk/client.py". For PR #2844, bumping first "CI still red after the fix. Same check failing." then adding an exception "CI green. Reviewer approved." For PR #7574, adding an exception directly in that legacy context "CI green. Reviewer approved."

For pip-audit failures where the log reports requests==2.31.0 vulnerable with fixed version 2.32.0, and the PR touches both a pinned dependency file (e.g., requirements.txt) and legacy SDK/client code, add a targeted pip-audit exception for the intentionally retained legacy requests pin rather than bumping the dependency. Do NOT apply this exception rule when the related changes are only in non-legacy application code (e.g., src/reports/export.py); in that case bump the requests pin to 2.32.0 instead. This was validated when legacy files were present (e.g., requirements.txt plus legacy_sdk/client.py), and misapplied when only non-legacy code changed (e.g., requirements.txt plus src/reports/export.py, where the reviewer said 'add audit exception is not how we do this here').

When CI fails in pip-audit with a vulnerable pinned dependency and the audit log names a fixed version, and the PR changes the requirements/lock file containing that pin, the default action is to bump the pin to the named fixed version rather than add an audit exception (reviewers have approved this when only the pin file changed).
Exception: if the PR also modifies legacy/compatibility-related code (e.g., legacy_sdk/*) suggesting the old pin is intentional, first try the bump; if CI remains red with the same pip-audit finding, add a scoped audit exception for the specific package/CVE.
Rationale and scope guardrails:
- Bump-only path held when the PR changed requirements.txt and unrelated code: on PR where files were "requirements.txt\nsrc/reports/export.py", bumping requests to the fixed 2.32.0 made CI green ("CI green. Reviewer approved.").
- Exception path is needed when legacy intent is present or the bump doesn’t clear the finding: on PRs where files were "requirements.txt\nlegacy_sdk/client.py", bumping left "CI still red after the fix. Same check failing." with the same log ("pip-audit: requests==2.31.0 has CVE-2024-XXXX; fix version 2.32.0"); adding a scoped exception then made CI green ("CI green. Reviewer approved.").
